extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy, and the scientific method
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for forming natural classifications (especially 'series' classifications) and a systematic taxonomy of fallacies — how to arrange kinds for inductive inquiry and how to identify and classify common modes of erroneous reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites of a classification intended to facilitate study of a particular phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: The classification must (1) bring into one class all kinds of things which exhibit the phenomenon, in whatever variety of forms or degrees; and (2) arrange those kinds in a series according to the degree in which they exhibit it, beginning with those which exhibit most and terminating with those which exhibit least.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the phenomenon under investigation as the groundwork of classification. The classification should group together for joint contemplation those instances most likely to throw light on the laws of that phenomenon (example: comparative anatomy for animal life).

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange instances according to the Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the instances, from which the law is to be inductively collected, into the order implied in the Method of Concomitant Variations: facts which increase or diminish together, and disappear together, are either cause and effect or effects of a common cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ordered series to detect concomitant changes; the series is a preparatory step required before applying the concomitant-variation inference with assurance. This ordering is often the only practicable method when artificial experiments cannot separate conjoined circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume a type-species when recognizing identity of a phenomenon across degrees
rubrics_metrics.description: To recognize exact similarity of a phenomenon in minute degrees with its highest development, the assumption of a type-species is indispensable: consider as the type the kind which exhibits the properties constitutive of the class in the highest degree, conceiving others as instances of degeneracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the phenomenon in its highest intensity where effects and joint effects are most discernible (example: man as type for studying animal life). This aids recognition of rudiments in less-developed instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground primary divisions on variations in degree of the main phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary divisions must be grounded not on all distinctions indiscriminately, but on those which correspond to variations in the degree of the main phenomenon; groups must not be so constituted as to place in the same group things which ought to occupy different points of the general scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the series at points where variation in intensity of the main phenomenon is attended by conspicuous changes in miscellaneous properties (examples: where Mammalia ends, where Fishes separate from Insects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal subdivision principle: families/genera should reflect contiguous positions in the series
rubrics_metrics.description: Each family, if possible, should be so subdivided that one portion stands higher and the other lower, though contiguous, in the general scale; only when this is impossible is it allowable to ground remaining subdivisions on characters without a determinable connection with the main phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer subdivisions that preserve ordinal position in the series; avoid rearrangements that mix distant points of the scale under the same subgroup unless forced by lack of connection to the main phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize the principal phenomenon when it transcends other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the principal phenomenon so far transcends in importance all other properties (as with animal life), classification should be framed with a reference to a natural series determined by that phenomenon, and groups formed according to the most important characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware of undue reference to secondary characters (example: Cuvier's undue emphasis on mode of alimentation); use those characters only when they truly correspond to positions in the scale of the main phenomenon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply principles of natural arrangement beyond natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: The same scientific conditions for forming groups and series apply to other extensive subjects (art, business, codes of law); proper arrangement depends on the same principles as in natural history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing material for a particular investigative or practical purpose (e.g., codification of laws), adopt the classification that best serves the intended inductive or utilitarian aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue varieties of apparent evidence (enumeration of fallacies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A catalogue of the varieties of apparent evidence which are not real evidence is an enumeration of Fallacies; without such an enumeration the theory of reasoning would be incomplete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey the different kinds of apparent evidence that can mislead (both those arising from facts and those arising from our mode of considering facts) to warn against common and dangerous forms of apparent conclusiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Habit of reasoning well as the principal safeguard against fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The only complete safeguard against reasoning ill is the habit of reasoning well: familiarity with the principles of correct reasoning and practice in applying those principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate continuous practice and disciplined application of inductive principles; mere recognition of fallacies is insufficient without the habit of exercising correct methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish moral from intellectual sources of error (focus on intellectual causes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sources of erroneous opinions are twofold: moral (indifference, bias) and intellectual. Moral causes operate indirectly by perverting the intellectual grounds of belief; a classification of non-evidence will include intellectual causes and thereby capture errors arising from moral causes as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate intellectual mechanisms (how evidence is processed) rather than only moral motivations; errors from bias or indifference typically manifest through intellectual failings (e.g., incomplete evidence-gathering, unequal attention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification principle for fallacies: by cause or by simulated evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fallacies may be arranged either according to the cause which makes them appear to be evidence (the special relation between facts) or according to the particular kind of evidence which they simulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use either axis (cause vs. simulated evidence) or both jointly to create a systematic taxonomy that reveals why an appearance of evidence arises and what legitimate form it mimics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori) from Fallacies of Inference
rubrics_metrics.description: First great distinction: Fallacies of Simple Inspection (a priori) include propositions believed without extrinsic evidence or held on presumption such that strict induction is dispensed with (natural prejudices). Fallacies of Inference are erroneous conclusions drawn from supposed evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a belief or argument determine whether it rests on mere inspection/presumption or on an asserted evidentiary process; remediate by requiring explicit evidence where presumption has been accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Confusion (shifting or ambiguous premises/language)
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors arising from not conceiving premises with due clearness or with due fixity: forming one conception of evidence when collected and another when used, unconsciously substituting different premises or conclusions — includes fallacies whose source is language (vagueness/ambiguity) or casual associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect by clarifying and fixing terms and by making implicit premises explicit; watch for equivocation and for covert shifts in meaning during an argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Induction: Observation (false facts) vs Generalization (true but inconclusive facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inductive fallacies subdivide: (a) Fallacies of Observation — when the facts on which induction proceeds are erroneous (malobservation or non-observation); (b) Fallacies of Generalization — when the observed facts are correct but do not warrant the general conclusion attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check the accuracy and completeness of observed facts (Observation), and assess whether the facts truly support the generalization intended (Generalization); consider sample size, representativeness, and alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacies of Deduction and Fallacies of Ratiocination
rubrics_metrics.description: Deductive fallacies arise when premises (general propositions) are used in a ratiocination; the class of fallacies proper to deduction are those in which the premises, though stated, do not bear out the conclusion — i.e., vicious argumentation countered by the rules of the syllogism (Fallacies of Ratiocination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate deductive arguments for validity: ensure the conclusion follows necessarily from the premises; identify invalid forms, illicit transference, or failure of premises to imply the conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many actual errors combine classes; expect suppressed premises
rubrics_metrics.description: Real-world erroneous arguments often mix kinds of fallacy and suppress links; in such arguments some links are tacit or omitted, and the error often lurks in those suppressed steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To detect the fallacy, supply the suppressed premise(s) that would be necessary to make the argument explicit; then test those premises for truth and sufficiency. Use Socratic interrogation or formal explication to force disclosure of implicit assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent evidentiary relation presupposes belief in habitual conjunction
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot regard one fact as evidentiary of another unless we believe that the two are always, or in the majority of cases, conjoined — i.e., the tendency to infer B from A rests on a presupposed general formula about their conjunction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When someone treats a sign as evidentiary, ask what general proposition about conjunction is being assumed; test whether the assumed regular conjunction holds or is groundless. This exposes the hidden generalization underlying the inference.
